title: Read compiler output and beat it by hand
brief: Write predicates over clang's assembly (loops, lea, memory traffic), compare -O0 with -O2, and hand-write a function that matches a C one.
hints: An instruction line is what is left after you strip comments (everything from # on) and whitespace, and drop labels (they end with a colon) and directives (they start with a dot).
The mnemonic is the first word of an instruction line. Compare it with lowercase text, because clang writes mnemonics in lowercase.
A loop in assembly is a jump that goes backward: the jump's target label appears earlier in the text than the jump. Record each label's line number, then check each jump.
Jump mnemonics start with j (jmp, jle, jne, ...). The target is the last word of the line.
For multiply by 5, `lea eax, [rdi + 4*rdi]` computes rdi + 4*rdi = 5*rdi. A regular expression with a back-reference, `(\w+)\s*\+\s*4\*\1`, matches the same register twice.
In score_asm, a*5 is one lea and b*8 is a shift (or another lea with a scale of 8). Write the 32-bit result into eax so it wraps like a C int.
